claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in spatial and contextual memory processes by forming cognitive maps of environments.
source: The hippocampus plays a critical role in spatial and contextual memory processes by forming cognitive maps of environments (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Moser et al., 2008; Lisman et al., 2017) that can support effective navigation toward learned salient locations (Robinson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Moser et al., 2008; Lisman et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2020

claim: During navigation, many pyramidal cells in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 area exhibit action potential firing that is restricted to spatial locations, the cell's place fields.
source: During navigation, many pyramidal cells (PCs) in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 area (CA1PCs) exhibit action potential (AP) firing that is restricted to spatial locations, the cell's place fields (PFs).
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about place cells in hippocampus

claim: In different environments, the activity of CA1PCs reorganizes to collectively form distinct representations, creating specific maps of each environment.
source: In different environments, the activity of CA1PCs reorganizes to collectively form distinct representations, that is creating specific maps of each environment.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about hippocampal remapping

claim: In a novel environment, many CA1PCs are active already during the first traversal of their PFs, but a fraction of cells become place cells after some delay.
source: In a novel environment, many CA1PCs are active already during the first traversal of their PFs, but a fraction of cells become place cells after some delay (Hill, 1978; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Frank et al., 2004; Epsztein et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 2017; Sheffield et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hill, 1978; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Frank et al., 2004; Epsztein et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 2017; Sheffield et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021

claim: Spatial maps gradually reorganize during continuous or repeated exploration of already familiar environments due to changes in the activity of individual PCs, including the recruitment of new place cells into the representation.
source: Furthermore, spatial maps also gradually reorganize during continuous or repeated exploration of already familiar environments due to changes in the activity of individual PCs, including the recruitment of new place cells into the representation (Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2021; Keinath et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2021; Keinath et al., 2022

claim: Recent in vivo patch-clamp recordings in head-fixed mice running on a familiar cue-rich treadmill revealed the spontaneous appearance of new PFs in previously silent cells, following the sudden occurrence of a robust, prolonged depolarization driving complex spike burst firing.
source: Most strikingly, in vivo patch-clamp recordings in head-fixed mice running on a familiar cue-rich treadmill revealed the spontaneous appearance of new PFs in previously silent cells, following the sudden occurrence of a robust, prolonged depolarization driving complex spike burst (CSB) firing (Bittner et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bittner et al., 2015

claim: Complex spike bursts are thought to be driven by dendritic Ca2+ spikes (plateau potentials) mediated by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and NMDA receptors.
source: Such CSBs are thought to be driven by dendritic Ca2+ spikes (plateau potentials) mediated by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and NMDA receptors (Takahashi and Magee, 2009; Grienberger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takahashi and Magee, 2009; Grienberger et al., 2014

claim: The formation of new PFs by plateau potentials is thought to be mediated by synaptic plasticity obeying a non-Hebbian rule, whereby the excitatory input synapses activated in a ~2-s-long time window around the CSB are rapidly potentiated.
source: The formation of new PFs by plateau potentials is thought to be mediated by synaptic plasticity obeying a non-Hebbian rule, whereby the excitatory input synapses activated in a ~2-s-long time window around the CSB are rapidly potentiated.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about BTSP mechanism

claim: This form of plasticity was named behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity (BTSP).
source: This form of plasticity was named behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity (BTSP; Bittner et al., 2017; Milstein et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bittner et al., 2017; Milstein et al., 2021

claim: Spontaneous PFF with BTSP-like characteristics was observed in CA1PCs by in vivo [Ca2+] imaging.
source: After initial electrophysiological demonstration, spontaneous PFF with BTSP-like characteristics was observed in CA1PCs by in vivo [Ca2+] imaging as well (Grienberger and Magee, 2022; Priestley et al., 2022; O'Hare et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grienberger and Magee, 2022; Priestley et al., 2022; O'Hare et al., 2025

claim: PFF with features similar to spontaneous BTSP-like PFF could be induced artificially by strong sustained electrical or optogenetic depolarization of a cell.
source: PFF with features similar to spontaneous BTSP-like PFF could also be induced artificially by strong sustained electrical or optogenetic depolarization of a cell (Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Milstein et al., 2021; Gonzalez et al., 2025; Rolotti et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2023), a stimulus assumed to evoke plateau potentials.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Milstein et al., 2021; Gonzalez et al., 2025; Rolotti et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2023

claim: In vivo patch-clamp recordings from CA1PCs in head-fixed mice running in a novel virtual environment showed that most of the delayed PFFs did not begin with CSBs, but with a weak subthreshold spatially tuned depolarization that increased when the PF emerged.
source: In vivo patch-clamp recordings (Cohen et al., 2017) from CA1PCs in head-fixed mice running in a novel virtual environment showed that most of the delayed PFFs did not begin with CSBs, but with a weak subthreshold spatially tuned depolarization that increased when the PF emerged.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2017

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of a small subset of CA1PCs at a particular location induced PFF or remapping in non-stimulated cells.
source: It has been shown that optogenetic stimulation of a small subset of CA1PCs at a particular location induced PFF or remapping in non-stimulated cells, suggesting that changes in synaptic coupling and circuit dynamics of PCs and inhibitory interneurons can also lead to reorganization of spatial maps by unmasking latent PFs (McKenzie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenzie et al., 2021

claim: Optogenetic induction of BTSP-like PFF has been shown to be restricted by lateral inhibition, strongly limiting the number of CA1PCs that can simultaneously form new PFs by BTSP.
source: Also pointing to a network effect, optogenetic induction of BTSP-like PFF has been shown to be restricted by lateral inhibition, strongly limiting the number of CA1PCs that can simultaneously form new PFs by BTSP (Rolotti et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolotti et al., 2022

claim: BTSP has several unique features when probed by somatic [Ca2+] imaging: the prolonged CSB results in large [Ca2+] transients during the initial PFF event, typically followed by weaker Ca2+ signals on consecutive traversals through the PF.
source: BTSP has several unique features when probed by somatic [Ca2+] imaging (Grienberger and Magee, 2022; Priestley et al., 2022). First, the prolonged CSB results in large [Ca2+] transients during the initial PFF event, typically followed by weaker Ca2+ signals on consecutive traversals through the PF.
evidence: Supported by citations to Grienberger and Magee, 2022; Priestley et al., 2022

claim: Due to the long and asymmetric temporal kernel of BTSP plasticity, a substantial backward shift in the spatial position of the PF center can be observed on linear tracks after the formation lap.
source: Second, due to the long and asymmetric temporal kernel of the plasticity (favoring potentiation of inputs active 1–2 s before the CSB), a substantial backward shift in the spatial position of the PF center can be observed on linear tracks after the formation lap.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about BTSP temporal kernel properties

claim: The width of the new PF formed by BTSP is generally proportional to the running speed of the animal during the PFF event.
source: Third, the width of the new PF is generally proportional to the running speed of the animal during the PFF event.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about BTSP properties

claim: In vivo two-photon [Ca2+] imaging of CA1PCs was performed from the dorsal hippocampus of head-restrained double transgenic mice (Thy1-GCaMP6s and Cre-dependent td-Tomato), injected with diluted Cre-recombinase expressing AAV.
source: In vivo two-photon [Ca2+] imaging of CA1PCs was performed from the dorsal hippocampus of head-restrained double transgenic mice (Thy1-GCaMP6s and Cre-dependent td-Tomato), injected with diluted Cre-recombinase expressing AAV (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Describes the experimental methods used in this study, shown in Figure 1A, B

claim: Mice were trained to run in an ~8-m-long virtual corridor for a water reward.
source: Mice were trained to run in an ~8-m-long virtual corridor for a water reward.
evidence: Describes the experimental setup used in this study

claim: The wall of the virtual corridor contained six well-discernible visual landmarks, the last of which indicated the reward zone.
source: The wall of the virtual corridor contained six well-discernible visual landmarks, the last of which indicated the reward zone (RZ), where mice were required to lick for water reward (Figure 1C).
evidence: Describes the experimental setup, shown in Figure 1C

claim: Well-trained mice ran with a relatively constant speed of ~30–40 cm/s through the corridor and slowed down and started licking just before entering the RZ.
source: Well-trained mice ran with a relatively constant speed of ~30–40 cm/s through the corridor and slowed down and started licking just before entering the RZ (Figure 1D), indicating that they learned the position of the RZ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Imaging was performed in well-trained mice across multiple days (n = 163 imaging sessions in 45 mice).
source: Imaging was performed in well-trained mice across multiple days (n = 163 imaging sessions in 45 mice).
evidence: Reports the sample size of the study

claim: The imaging field of view contained ~1000 CA1PC somata.
source: The imaging field of view contained ~1000 CA1PC somata (Figure 1B), which showed highly variable activities during the session (Figure 1E–H); some cells were silent whereas others showed moderate to high activity rates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, E-H

claim: The PFs of place cells tiled the entire length of the corridor with an increased density around the visual landmarks.
source: The PFs of place cells tiled the entire length of the corridor with an increased density around the visual landmarks (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J

claim: The activity of CA1PCs in the experimental conditions is comparable to that observed in animals exploring large environments.
source: These results demonstrate that the activity of CA1PCs in our experimental conditions is comparable to that observed in animals exploring large environments (Rich et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2020; Eliav et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with cited studies (Rich et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2020; Eliav et al., 2021)

claim: During navigation in the familiar virtual corridor, new PFs often appeared suddenly at various spatial locations during the session.
source: During navigation in the familiar virtual corridor, new PFs often appeared suddenly at various spatial locations during the session (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: 311 new PFs were categorized as formed by a BTSP-like mechanism (having both positive gain and negative shift values).
source: Using a conservative approach, we categorized a new PF to be formed by a BTSP-like mechanism if it had both positive gain and negative shift values (Figure 2A; n = 311 new PFs), whereas new PFs exhibiting neither positive gain nor negative shift were considered as non-BTSP-like events (Figure 2B; n = 58).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: 58 new PFs were categorized as non-BTSP-like events (exhibiting neither positive gain nor negative shift).
source: Using a conservative approach, we categorized a new PF to be formed by a BTSP-like mechanism if it had both positive gain and negative shift values (Figure 2A; n = 311 new PFs), whereas new PFs exhibiting neither positive gain nor negative shift were considered as non-BTSP-like events (Figure 2B; n = 58).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: A bootstrap analysis demonstrated that misclassification of non-BTSP-like PFF events due to random Ca2+ activity is unlikely for the majority (88%) of non-BTSP-like new PFF events.
source: However, a bootstrap analysis (see Methods) demonstrated that this is unlikely for the majority (88%) of non-BTSP-like new PFF events (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: In a visually complex VR environment without dominant visual landmarks, BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFF events were readily observed with a very similar proportion to that observed in the original VR environment.
source: Here, BTSP- (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, n = 117 event from 12 imaging sessions from 4 mice) and non-BTSP-like (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, n = 18) PFF events were readily observed with a very similar proportion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G) to that observed in our original VR environment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-G

claim: Apart from the strongly different [Ca2+] amplitudes in the formation lap, [Ca2+] transients within the PF on the subsequent laps had similar amplitudes between BTSP-like and non-BTSP-like new PFs.
source: Comparison of the [Ca2+] transients of BTSP-like (n = 311) and non-BTSP-like (n = 58) new PFs in the laps before, during, and after their formation showed that, apart from the strongly different [Ca2+] amplitudes in the formation lap, [Ca2+] transients within the PF on the subsequent laps had similar amplitudes (Figure 2C, D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: The amplitude of the [Ca2+] transients in the formation lap is significantly higher during BTSP-like compared to non-BTSP-like PFFs.
source: Statistical analysis revealed that the amplitude of the [Ca2+] transients in the formation lap is significantly higher during BTSP-like compared to non-BTSP-like PFFs and the amplitudes in the other laps are not significantly different (mixed ANOVA: main effect for group (BTSP/non-BTSP): p = 0.038; lap: p < 0.001, interaction: p < 0.001; Tukey post hoc test: formation lap: p < 0.001, all other laps: p > 0.711).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The basic characteristics of activity in the stabilized new PFs (widths, peak rates, out-of-field firing rates, fractions of active laps) were comparable between BTSP-like and non-BTSP-like groups.
source: fractions of active laps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), widths (BTSP: 46.4 ± 24.4 cm; non-BTSP: 50.4 ± 32.5 cm, p = 0.28), peak rates (BTSP: 19.0 ± 14.7 a.u./s; non-BTSP: 21.4 ± 16.8 a.u./s, p = 0.27) and out-of-field firing rates (BTSP: 0.64 ± 0.68 a.u./s; non-BTSP: 0.83 ± 1.25 a.u./s, p = 0.09, all unpaired t-test), indicating that the basic characteristics of activity in the stabilized new PFs were comparable between the two groups.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Both types of new PFs exhibited similar distributions along the virtual track, tiling the whole corridor with increased densities around the visual landmarks.
source: Furthermore, both types of new PFs exhibited similar distributions along the virtual track, tiling the whole corridor with increased densities around the visual landmarks (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between formation lap running speed and PF width in the BTSP-like but not in the non-BTSP-like PF category.
source: As an independent confirmation that newly formed PFs in our categorization of PF groups genuinely differed in the mechanisms underlying their formation, we found a significant positive correlation between formation lap running speed and PF width in the BTSP-like but not in the non-BTSP-like PF category (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B (Spearman correlations: BTSP (n = 261): R = 0.29, p = 2.7 × 10–6; non-BTSP (n = 47): R = 0.015, p = 0.92)

claim: The animal's distance to the closest visual landmark center significantly correlated with PF width for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFFs.
source: We found that the animal's distance to the closest visual landmark center significantly correlated with PF width for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFFs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C (Spearman correlations: BTSP (n = 261): R = 0.59, p = 1.4 × 10–25; non-BTSP (n = 47): R = 0.67, p = 2.4 × 10–7)

claim: Cue distance explained a similarly large fraction of the PF width variance for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFFs, whereas speed explained a moderate proportion of PF width variance only in the case of BTSP-like PFFs.
source: Considering the effects of both speed and cue distance, we found that cue distance explained a similarly large fraction of the PF width variance for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFFs, whereas speed explained a moderate proportion of PF width variance only in the case of BTSP-like PFFs (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: In most sessions, the number of newly formed PFs was moderate, but a few sessions contained unusually large numbers of such events.
source: While in most of the sessions, the number of newly formed PFs was moderate, a few sessions contained unusually large numbers of such events (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: In sessions with unusually large numbers of PFF events, the majority of PFF events occurred within a short period over a limited number (3–10) of consecutive laps.
source: When we examined the distribution of new PFFs in these sessions across individual laps, we found that the majority of PFF events occurred within a short period over a limited number (3–10) of consecutive laps (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Concentrated PFF periods (PFF 'surges') included PFs formed both by BTSP- and non-BTSP-like mechanisms (non-BTSP: 22 events; BTSP: 40 events, non-BTSP/BTSP ratio: 0.55).
source: These concentrated PFF periods were termed PFF 'surges', which included PFs formed both by BTSP- and non-BTSP-like mechanisms (non-BTSP: 22 events; BTSP: 40 events, non-BTSP/BTSP ratio: 0.55).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: The lap-by-lap correlation of activity in the whole population of imaged CA1PCs underwent a drastic and rapid switch between two stable states before and after the PFF surge.
source: Indeed, we found that the lap-by-lap correlation of activity in the whole population of imaged CA1PCs underwent a drastic and rapid switch between two stable states before and after the PFF surge (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The remapping was essentially global, as only a small fraction (5.4%) of CA1PCs retained their pre-switch tuning curve after the switch.
source: The remapping was essentially global, as only a small fraction (5.4%) of CA1PCs retained their pre-switch tuning curve after the switch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: The [Ca2+] dynamics of PFFs during surges were similar to those of PFFs outside the surges for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like groups, except for larger [Ca2+] signals in the first lap after the formation lap in the non-BTSP group during surges compared to outside surges.
source: When we compared the [Ca2+] dynamics of PFFs during surges with those of PFFs outside the surges, we found similar [Ca2+] amplitudes in both the BTSP- and non-BTSP-like groups, except for larger [Ca2+] signals in the first lap after the formation lap in the non-BTSP group during surges compared to outside surges (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G, H

claim: The period including the PFF surge and representational switch was not accompanied by any noticeable change in the behavioral performance of the animals as assessed by running speed and lick rate.
source: The period including the PFF surge and representational switch was not accompanied by any noticeable change in the behavioral performance of the animals as assessed by running speed and lick rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Multiday imaging revealed that in some animals, switching between the same two representations occurred on consecutive days.
source: Furthermore, multiday imaging revealed that in some animals, switching between the same two representations occurred on consecutive days (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), and occasionally, multiple representation switches within one imaging session could be observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E

claim: The familiar virtual corridor was extended with a 6-m-long segment decorated with never-seen visual landmarks during the imaging session.
source: We next sought to determine the contribution of BTSP- and non-BTSP-like mechanisms to new PFFs in a novel environment by extending the familiar virtual corridor with a 6-m-long segment decorated with never-seen visual landmarks during the imaging session (Figure 4A).
evidence: Describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 4A

claim: Population-level analysis revealed a reorganization of the neuronal representation, as demonstrated by a decreased population vector correlation between the extended and original maze, despite high intra-segment correlations.
source: Population-level analysis revealed a reorganization of the neuronal representation, as demonstrated by a decreased population vector (PV) correlation between the extended and original maze, despite high intra-segment correlations (mean correlation coefficients: original maze odd vs. even: 0.50 ± 0.19, original maze odd vs. extended maze even: 0.08 ± 0.10, extended maze odd vs. even: 0.36 ± 0.20; n = 6 mice; repeated measures ANOVA (p < 0.001) followed by Tukey post hoc test: original maze odd − even vs. original maze odd − extended maze even: p < 0.001, extended maze odd − even vs. original maze odd − extended maze even: p = 0.002, original maze odd − even vs. extended maze odd − even: p = 0.114).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Many new PFs were observed already during the first traversal in the novel extension of the virtual environment, and additional new PFs formed during subsequent laps, although with lower probability.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Sheffield et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021; Priestley et al., 2022), we observed many new PFs already during the first traversal in the novel extension of the virtual environment, and additional new PFs formed during subsequent laps, although with lower probability (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and citations to Sheffield et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021; Priestley et al., 2022

claim: The frequency of new PFFs was the highest in the first few laps for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like events in the novel environment.
source: The frequency of new PFFs was the highest in the first few laps for both BTSP- and non-BTSP-like events (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The amplitudes of somatic [Ca2+] transients during the formation lap were very similar between the novel and familiar environments for both the BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFF events.
source: Analysis of the somatic [Ca2+] transients revealed that their amplitudes were very similar to those observed in the familiar environment for both the BTSP- and non-BTSP-like PFF events during the formation lap (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: In subsequent laps of the novel corridor, BTSP-like PFF dominated again (non-BTSP/BTSP ratio = 0.15).
source: whereas in the subsequent laps BTSP-like PFF dominated again (novel corridor region, laps 3–31: non-BTSP/BTSP ratio = 0.15).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: In approximately one quarter of the sessions, BTSP-inducing [Ca2+] transients could be matched with at least one larger [Ca2+] transient that failed to initiate new PFF ('solitary events').
source: We found that, in approximately one quarter of the sessions, BTSP-inducing [Ca2+] transients could be matched with at least one larger [Ca2+] transient that failed to initiate new PFF ('solitary events', Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: The amplitudes of [Ca2+] transients of the solitary events in the event lap were significantly higher, whereas in the lap after the event lap they were smaller compared to those of BTSP-like events.
source: The amplitudes of [Ca2+] transients of the solitary events in the event lap were significantly higher, whereas in the EL+1 they were smaller compared to those of BTSP-like events (mixed ANOVA: main effect for group (BTSP/solitary): p = 0.682, lap: p < 0.001, interaction: p < 0.001; Tukey post hoc test: lap –1: p = 1, event lap: p < 0.001, lap +1: p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Although many PFs are formed by BTSP-like events, PFs also emerge with initial [Ca2+] dynamics that do not match any of the characteristics of BTSP.
source: Our results demonstrate that although many PFs are formed by BTSP-like events, PFs also emerge with initial [Ca2+] dynamics that do not match any of the characteristics of BTSP.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data presented in the study

claim: BTSP- and non-BTSP-like new PFFs occur spontaneously in familiar environments, during neuronal representational switches, and instantaneously in new environments.
source: BTSP- and non-BTSP-like new PFFs occur spontaneously in familiar environments, during neuronal representational switches, and instantaneously in new environments.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data presented in the study

claim: Solitary [Ca2+] transients with larger amplitudes than those evoking BTSP-like PFFs frequently occur without inducing PFs, demonstrating that large [Ca2+] transients per se are not sufficient for PFF.
source: Our data also reveal that solitary [Ca2+] transients with larger amplitudes than those evoking BTSP-like PFFs frequently occur without inducing PFs, demonstrating that large [Ca2+] transients per se are not sufficient for PFF.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data presented in the study

claim: BTSP is prevalent but is not the only mechanism driving PFFs, as many new PFs formed without exhibiting any of the characteristics of BTSP.
source: We find that BTSP is prevalent but is not the only mechanism driving PFFs, as many new PFs formed without exhibiting any of the characteristics of BTSP.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data presented in the study

claim: Robust CSB-like somatic activity is often ineffective in inducing new PFs, suggesting that additional factors are required than just CSBs to successfully initiate new PFs.
source: Furthermore, we show that robust CSB-like somatic activity is often ineffective in inducing new PFs, suggesting that additional factors are required than just CSBs to successfully initiate new PFs.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data presented in the study

claim: The lack of large initial somatic [Ca2+] transients during non-BTSP-like PFFs suggests they either do not involve excitatory synaptic plasticity in CA1PCs but rather result from a change in incoming excitatory or inhibitory synaptic inputs, or they are driven by other synaptic plasticity mechanisms that do not require global Ca2+ plateaus and CSBs.
source: The lack of large initial somatic [Ca2+] transients – that are likely associated with strong bursts involving Ca2+ plateaus – during non-BTSP-like PFFs suggests two possible scenarios: they either do not involve excitatory synaptic plasticity in CA1PCs but rather result from a change in incoming excitatory or inhibitory synaptic inputs, or they are driven by other synaptic plasticity mechanisms that do not require global Ca2+ plateaus and CSBs to increase excitatory synaptic weights.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Local synaptic plasticity in individual dendritic branches is a particularly intriguing possibility for non-BTSP-like PFF, since PFF can be preceded by local dendritic activity at the future PF locations.
source: Local synaptic plasticity in individual dendritic branches is a particularly intriguing possibility for the latter scenario, since it has been shown that PFF can be preceded by local dendritic activity at the future PF locations (Sheffield et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to Sheffield et al., 2017

claim: Long-term potentiation of excitatory synaptic inputs by local dendritic Na+ and/or NMDA spikes can be induced by a single or a few repetitions of d-spikes.
source: Importantly, long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory synaptic inputs by local dendritic Na+ and/or NMDA spikes (d-spikes) can be induced by a single or a few repetitions of d-spikes (Remy and Spruston, 2007; Magó et al., 2020), and thus can be consistent with rapid generation of new PFs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Remy and Spruston, 2007; Magó et al., 2020

claim: BTSP dominates PFFs under conditions when new PFs are born in individual CA1PCs that are part of a relatively stable representation in a familiar environment, i.e. during gradual representational drift.
source: We found that BTSP dominates PFFs under conditions when new PFs are born in individual CA1PCs that are part of a relatively stable representation in a familiar environment, i.e. during gradual representational drift.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data analysis

claim: The relative ratio of non-BTSP-like PFF was much higher in the first laps of a novel corridor segment, which may be consistent with a global remapping process.
source: In contrast, the relative ratio of non-BTSP-like PFF was much higher in the first laps of a novel corridor segment. This may be consistent with a global remapping process in response to reconfiguration of the excitatory input patterns arriving to individual CA1PCs from upstream areas.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data analysis

claim: The higher ratio of non-BTSP- to BTSP-like PFFs in the initial laps of the novel environment and during representational switches (both ~0.60) than that in the familiar environment (0.19) suggests that distinct cellular/synaptic mechanisms might contribute to gradual representational drifts and abrupt global remapping.
source: Overall, the higher ratio of non-BTSP- to BTSP-like PFFs in the initial laps of the novel environment and during representational switches (both ~0.60) than that in the familiar environment (0.19) suggests that distinct cellular/synaptic mechanisms might contribute to gradual representational drifts and abrupt global remapping.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data analysis

claim: Large somatic Ca2+ signals that fail to induce PFF indicate either that the synaptic plasticity induced by the underlying plateau was not sufficiently strong to lead to somatic firing, or that the induction of plasticity may be gated by additional factor(s), for example modulatory signals or inhibition.
source: If we assume that the large (and often prolonged) somatic Ca2+ signals represent CSBs, this indicates either that the synaptic plasticity induced by the underlying plateau was not sufficiently strong to lead to somatic firing (perhaps influenced by head-fixed VR navigation with diminished sensory cues, Ravassard et al., 2013), or that the induction of plasticity may be gated by additional factor(s), for example modulatory signals or inhibition.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings, with citation to Ravassard et al., 2013

claim: A total of 45 (23 male and 22 female) Ai9xGP4.3 double-transgenic mice were used in this study.
source: A total of 45 (23 male and 22 female) Ai9xGP4.3 double-transgenic mice were used in this study.
evidence: Reports the sample characteristics of the study

source: In our initial categorization of PFFs detected in the standard maze (Figures 1 and 2), we found 806 candidate BTSP-like (52%) and 164 non-BTSP-like (10%) PFFs; an additional 593 PFs (38%) could not be included in the above two groups [40 PFs (3%) with formation lap gain and backward shift but significant backward drift; 238 PFs (15%) with formation lap gain but without backward shift; 315 PFs (20%) with no formation lap gain but with backward shift]; these PFs were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: Reports the categorization results of the data analysis

claim: A conservative approach was employed for categorizing PFFs: only PFF events that fulfilled all criteria of either BTSP- or non-BTSP-like groups were included in the analysis, and PFFs that failed on at least one criterion were excluded.
source: We emphasize that we employed a conservative approach for categorizing PFFs: we only included PFF events in our analysis if they fulfilled all criteria of either BTSP- or non-BTSP-like groups and excluded PFFs that failed on at least one criterion.
evidence: Describes the data analysis approach used
